{{Short description|Topological theorem}}
In the mathematical field of [[differential geometry]], the '''Osserman–Xavier–Fujimoto theorem''' concerns the [[Gauss map]]s of [[minimal surface]]s in the three-dimensional [[Euclidean space]]. It says that if a minimal surface is [[Immersion (mathematics)|immersed]] and [[geodesically complete]], then the image of the Gauss map either consists of a single point (so that the surface is a plane) or contains all of the sphere except for at most four points.

[[Bernstein's problem|Bernstein's theorem]] says that a minimal ''graph'' in {{math|'''R'''<sup>3</sup>}} which is geodesically complete must be a plane. This can be rephrased to say that the Gauss map of a complete immersed minimal surface in {{math|'''R'''<sup>3</sup>}} is either constant or not contained within an open hemisphere. As [[conjecture]]d by [[Louis Nirenberg]] and proved by [[Robert Osserman]] in 1959, in this form Bernstein's theorem can be generalized to say that the image of the Gauss map of a complete immersed minimal surface in {{math|'''R'''<sup>3</sup>}} either consists of a single point or is [[dense set|dense]] within the sphere.{{sfnm|1a1=Lawson|1y=1980|1loc=Section III.5|2a1=Nitsche|2y=1965|2loc=Section V.1|3a1=Osserman|3y=1986|3loc=Section 8}}

Osserman's theorem was improved by Frederico Xavier and Hirotaka Fujimoto in the 1980s. They proved that if the image of the Gauss map of a complete immersed minimal surface in {{math|'''R'''<sup>3</sup>}} omits more than four points of the sphere, then the surface is a plane.{{sfnm|1a1=Dierkes|1a2=Hildebrandt|1a3=Küster|1a4=Wohlrab|1y=1992|1loc=Theorem 3.7.1}} This is optimal, since it was shown by [[Konrad Voss]] in the 1960s that for any subset {{mvar|A}} of the sphere whose complement consists of zero, one, two, three, or four points, there exists a complete immersed minimal surface in {{math|'''R'''<sup>3</sup>}} whose Gauss map has image {{mvar|A}}.{{sfnm|1a1=Dierkes|1a2=Hildebrandt|1a3=Küster|1a4=Wohlrab|1y=1992|1loc=Proposition 3.7.4|2a1=Nitsche|2y=1965|2loc=Section V.1.5|3a1=Osserman|3y=1986|3loc=Section 8}} Particular examples include [[Riemann's minimal surface]], whose Gauss map is surjective, the [[Enneper surface]], whose Gauss map omits one point, the [[catenoid]] and [[helicoid]], whose Gauss maps omit two points, and [[Scherk surface|Scherk's first surface]], whose Gauss map omits four points.

It is also possible to study the Gauss map of minimal surfaces of higher [[codimension]] in higher-dimensional Euclidean spaces. There are a number of variants of the results of Osserman, Xavier, and Fujimoto which can be studied in this setting.{{sfnm|1a1=Chen|1y=2000|1loc=Section 5.6.2|2a1=Yau|2y=1993|2loc=Problem 33}}
